title: Student submission metadata can enable cross-context linkage
description: The flow carries student id, course, submission timestamp, and assignment file into the portal. If P1 uses persistent identifiers and precise timestamps across courses or services, records from different submissions can be linked to build a broader profile of the student’s behavior and academic activity.
assumptions: Assumes the portal stores or reuses stable student identifiers and fine-grained timestamps beyond what is strictly necessary for accepting the submission.
uncertainty_note: Tree node id is best-judgement because the retrieved context only gave threat-type applicability, not detailed tree nodes.

title: Assignment upload reveals student identity and course participation
description: The submitted data directly identifies the student and reveals that they participate in a specific course and submitted work at a specific time. If the flow is observable by unauthorized parties or exposed through weak access controls, sensitive academic information is disclosed.
assumptions: Assumes there is some risk of interception, over-broad internal access, or insufficient protection of incoming request data and logs.
uncertainty_note: Detailed tree node selection is approximate; the applicability of information disclosure to this flow is high.

title: Student may be unable to prove or dispute assignment submission
description: If P1 does not generate trustworthy evidence such as a receipt, signed acknowledgment, or tamper-evident audit trail, the student could later be unable to prove that a submission was made on time, or the portal could be unable to prove what was submitted.
assumptions: Assumes submission handling may lack strong confirmation and integrity-protected logging.
uncertainty_note: Tree node id is approximate; non-repudiation concerns clearly apply to assignment submission flows.

title: Submission contents and metadata expose student behavior
description: The uploaded work file, course, student id, and timestamp allow inference about the student’s study patterns, deadlines met or missed, workload, and possibly special-category information if assignment content contains personal details. Even without explicit disclosure, observing or analyzing this flow can reveal private facts.
assumptions: Assumes the assignment content or timing is accessible to parties who do not need it, or is mined for secondary purposes.

uncertainty_note: Applies especially if transport metadata, URL patterns, or timing are exposed; exact tree node is best-judgement.

title: Student may be unaware of secondary use or retention of submitted work

This creates an unawareness threat around processing purposes, recipients, and retention.
assumptions: Assumes privacy notices or just-in-time explanations are incomplete or not salient at submission time.
uncertainty_note: Unawareness is strongly plausible for this flow, though the exact tree node id is approximate.

title: Submission processing may exceed consent or legitimate expectation
description: If P1 processes the assignment file and metadata for purposes beyond accepting and grading the submission—such as profiling, model training, broad analytics, or excessive retention—without an appropriate legal basis or honoring user choices, the flow creates a non-compliance risk.

assumptions: Assumes the system does not automatically notify or otherwise inform affected users of administrative changes involving their personal data.
uncertainty_note: Applies at the process receiving and enacting the changes; exact subtree id is approximate.

title: Administrative management of parent-child links may lack lawful basis or consent handling
description: Parent-child relationship data can be especially sensitive in an educational context. If the portal allows administrators to create or alter these links without verifying the appropriate legal basis, authorization, or consent/guardian-status requirements, the processing may be non-compliant with privacy obligations.
assumptions: Assumes jurisdiction or policy requires a valid legal basis, authorization, or consent workflow for establishing family relationships in the system.
uncertainty_note: Compliance obligations depend on jurisdiction and school policy; exact node id is best-judgement.

title: Linkability via persistent parent-child relationship links in the account directory
description: Writing parent-child relationship links into a central account directory can enable records for students, parents, and related account events to be linked across contexts and over time. If the directory uses stable identifiers or exposes relationship edges broadly, observers or internal actors may correlate educational, household, and account-management activities.
assumptions: The account directory stores stable account identifiers and explicit parent-child relationship references that may be reused by multiple services or administrators.
uncertainty_note: Tree-node id is based on general LINDDUN Pro linkability categorization; exact sub-node may vary by threat-tree version.

title: Identifiability of students and parents through directory records
description: Account records combined with parent-child relationship links can directly identify a child and their parent/guardian, or make re-identification straightforward even if some fields are pseudonymous. The directory becomes a strong identity resolution point for family relationships.
assumptions: Account records contain direct identifiers or quasi-identifiers, and the relationship link is stored in a way accessible to systems or staff beyond the minimum necessary scope.
uncertainty_note: Exact node id may differ depending on whether the threat tree distinguishes direct identification from indirect re-identification.

title: Detectability of family relationship existence from directory writes
description: The act of writing or updating parent-child relationship links may allow an observer with access to logs, metadata, or the directory state to detect that a specific student has an associated parent account, or that a relationship was newly created or changed. Even without reading full record contents, the existence of the relationship may be privacy-sensitive.
assumptions: Write operations, metadata, timestamps, or record presence are observable to administrators, operators, or other components.
uncertainty_note: Applies if metadata or record existence is observable; if writes are fully opaque and tightly access-controlled, impact is reduced.

title: Detectability of grading-service activity through account-directory updates
description: Because the grading service writes account records and relationship links, updates in the directory may reveal when grading-related onboarding, enrollment, or account-maintenance events occur. This can expose operational patterns about students or families even if content is not disclosed.
assumptions: Directory update timing can be correlated with grading-service operations by someone who can observe datastore changes or logs.
uncertainty_note: This is a metadata-based detectability threat and depends on observability of update timing.

title: Disclosure of sensitive family relationship data in the account directory
description: The flow stores parent-child relationship links and account records in the directory. Unauthorized access, overbroad internal access, or secondary use of this datastore could disclose sensitive personal data about minors, guardians, and their associations.
assumptions: The directory is accessible by multiple services, administrators, or support personnel, or may be queried beyond the immediate grading use case.

title: Unawareness of storage and reuse of parent-child links
description: Students and parents may be unaware that the grading service writes their account records and family relationship links into a central account directory, potentially for reuse by other services or administrative functions. This can undermine transparency about what data is stored, where, and for what purposes.
assumptions: Notices or UI disclosures do not clearly explain this write operation, the directory's role, retention, or downstream consumers.
uncertainty_note: This is inferred from the architecture; actual applicability depends on provided privacy notices and user-facing explanations.

title: Non-compliance risk from storing child-parent relationship data without adequate purpose limitation or minimization
description: Persisting account records together with parent-child relationship links in a central directory may exceed what is necessary for grading if fields, retention, or sharing are broader than required. Because the data concerns minors and family relationships, inadequate legal basis, transparency, retention control, or access limitation could create compliance issues.
assumptions: Applicable law or policy imposes heightened requirements for children's data, family relationship data, retention limits, and purpose limitation.
uncertainty_note: Compliance obligations depend on jurisdiction and organizational policy; exact legal exposure cannot be determined from the DFD alone.

title: Excessive disclosure of student and staff personal data to third-party cloud host
description: The nightly backup/replication sends full grade records, assignments, and the account directory to an external cloud hosting provider. This may disclose more personal data than is strictly necessary for backup/hosting purposes, especially if full records are replicated rather than minimized, segmented, or pseudonymized.
assumptions: The cloud hosting provider is a separate third party and receives or can access the replicated backup contents in identifiable form.
uncertainty_note: Tree node id is based on best judgement for unnecessary/excessive third-party disclosure; exact subnode may vary by LINDDUN Pro version.

title: Disclosure of sensitive educational data across a trust boundary
description: Grade records and assignment content are transferred from the service to an external entity, crossing an organizational boundary. These datasets can contain sensitive educational performance data and identifiers, creating a privacy threat if the transfer is avoidable, insufficiently scoped, or exposes data to personnel or subprocessors at the provider.
assumptions: The provider is outside the primary system trust boundary and the replicated data includes personal data linked to identifiable users.
uncertainty_note: Exact threat-tree subnode for boundary-crossing disclosure may differ; classification as Data Disclosure is strong.

title: Third-party backup replication may be incompatible with user expectations or stated purposes
description: Users may provide assignment submissions, grades, and directory information for educational administration, but may not reasonably expect full replication of that data to a third-party cloud host. If this onward transfer is not aligned with the original purpose, notice, consent, contract, or other legal basis, the flow creates a non-compliance threat.
assumptions: Applicable policy, notice, contract, or legal basis may restrict onward transfer or require transparency and safeguards for cloud hosting.
uncertainty_note: Specific compliance obligations depend on jurisdiction and organizational commitments; tree node id is best-effort.

title: Full backup replication enables over-identification by the hosting provider
description: Replicating complete grade records together with assignments and the account directory gives the cloud provider enough direct and contextual identifiers to single out and identify individual students or staff. Even if some fields were partially masked elsewhere, the combined dataset can re-identify data subjects.
assumptions: The replicated dataset contains names, account identifiers, or linkable directory attributes alongside educational records.
uncertainty_note: Exact Unawareness/Identifiability subnode may vary; identifiability risk from combined full datasets is clear.

title: Replicated backups can link educational records with directory identities
description: Sending full grade records, assignments, and the account directory together allows the recipient to link academic performance, submitted work, and account identity into unified profiles. This increases the ability to correlate data across contexts beyond what is necessary for infrastructure hosting.
assumptions: The provider can access or process all replicated datasets together rather than only encrypted blobs without metadata access.
uncertainty_note: Tree node id is best-effort; the core threat is linkability created by combining multiple datasets in one transfer.

title: Linkability of grade records across audiences
description: The grading service reads the same grade records to build student, parent, and teacher views. If identifiers or stable record keys are reused across these views, the service can link a student's performance data across contexts and recipients, enabling correlation of activities and outcomes beyond what each audience strictly needs.
assumptions: P2 generates or serves distinct views for multiple roles from the same underlying records and may reuse persistent identifiers across them.
uncertainty_note: Tree node is best-judgement because the retrieved context only gives applicable threat types, not detailed node ids.

title: Identifiability of students in retrieved grade data
description: Grade records are likely directly associated with student identities or easily identifying attributes. When P2 reads these records to assemble views, individuals may be directly identifiable to recipients or internal operators even where only performance status or limited educational information is necessary.
assumptions: Grade records contain names, student IDs, class membership, or other quasi-identifiers.
uncertainty_note: Specific node id is approximate due to missing detailed threat-tree mapping in the provided context.

title: Excess disclosure of grade details to role-specific views
description: Because P2 builds views for students, parents, and teachers from the same database read, there is a risk that the service discloses more grade information than necessary for a given role, such as exposing detailed assessment history, comments, or other students' information through overly broad queries or insufficient output filtering.
assumptions: Role-based filtering or field-level minimization may be incomplete or misconfigured.
uncertainty_note: Threat is grounded in the described multi-audience read path; exact tree node id is approximate.

title: Unawareness of secondary use of grade records for multiple audiences
description: Students may not be aware that their grade records are read and repurposed by the grading service to construct separate parent and teacher views, potentially including derived summaries or contextual information beyond the original grading purpose.
assumptions: Data subjects were not clearly informed that the same records would be reused across multiple stakeholder views.
uncertainty_note: Applies if transparency notices are incomplete; this cannot be confirmed from the flow alone.

title: Inability to intervene in propagated grade-view data
description: Once P2 reads grade records and builds downstream views for different audiences, a student may have limited ability to challenge, correct, or restrict dissemination of inaccurate or outdated grade information before it is shown to parents or teachers.
assumptions: The service lacks timely correction, objection, or suppression mechanisms tied to view generation.
uncertainty_note: This depends on governance and user-rights mechanisms not visible in the DFD, so applicability is moderate-confidence.

title: Role-inappropriate processing of grade records without adequate legal basis or policy alignment
description: Reading grade records to build student, parent, and teacher views may process personal data in ways that exceed the original educational purpose or violate policy/legal constraints if access scopes, parental entitlements, age thresholds, or institutional rules are not properly enforced by P2.
assumptions: Different audiences have different lawful access rights and purpose limitations for educational records.
uncertainty_note: Non-compliance depends on jurisdictional and institutional rules not provided in the prompt.
